Telemetry Requirements

Putting the evidence into the specification: what a feature must emit, where it must emit it from, and why the enumerated events are simultaneously the only thing that will settle an argument and the most reliable way to be confidently wrong.

1Two decisions, one week apart

On the morning of 9 February 2026, Devyani Rao, Director of Product for Connected Appliances at Aamap Instruments in Pune, sat with a firmware lead and a service-operations manager in front of a whiteboard containing a single unresolved column. Aamap builds connected water-treatment and air-quality appliances for Indian households — 12.4 lakh units in the field, of which 7.9 lakh carry an annual filter-and-service plan priced at ₹2,400, giving the service business roughly ₹190 crore of recurring revenue. Renewal on that plan runs at 71 percent, and the single strongest predictor of renewal, across three years of retrospective analysis, is whether the household replaced its filter on time in the preceding cycle. Each percentage point of renewal is worth about ₹1.9 crore a year. The feature on the whiteboard, Predictive Filter Alert, replaced the calendar reminder Aamap had used since 2019 — a notification sent 180 days after the last service, regardless of use — with an estimate derived from the appliance's own measurements: litres processed, inlet total dissolved solids, and flow-rate decay, converted into a predicted exhaustion date and surfaced eleven days ahead with a one-tap booking. The engineering was, by Aamap's standards, straightforward. The column Devyani could not fill was headed: what will tell us, by 30 April, whether this worked?

The difficulty was not that nobody had ideas. It was that every idea collided with a physical fact. Aamap's installed base runs three firmware generations. The 4.x fleet — 62 percent of connected units, skewed towards metros and towards households who bought in the last thirty months — has a general-purpose telemetry channel, an over-the-air update path and, in most homes, a companion mobile app. The 3.x fleet, 38 percent of units and disproportionately in tier-two and tier-three towns, communicates over a narrowband cellular module with a data allowance measured in kilobytes per day and a firmware image that cannot be extended without a physical service visit. Devyani's instinct, and her instrumentation engineer's proposal, was to define a rich event contract: an alert issued, an alert seen, a booking started, a booking confirmed, a technician dispatched, a filter replaced. Her operations manager pointed out the obvious problem. If the rich contract exists only on 4.x, then the experiment measures the behaviour of metro households with smartphones and good connectivity — precisely the households least likely to let a filter lapse — and the resulting number, however precisely computed, would answer a question nobody at Aamap was asking. "We will have a clean read," he said, "on the segment that never had the problem."

Three days later and 840 kilometres away, on 12 February, Arjun Menon convened a different argument in a fourth-floor conference room in Bengaluru. Menon is Group Product Manager at Ankan Support Cloud, an AI-native platform that reads a customer-support ticket, retrieves the relevant policy and order state through tool calls, and drafts a resolution. Sixty-four enterprise accounts, ₹41 crore of annual recurring revenue, 11.4 lakh tickets processed a month. The feature under review, Autonomous Resolve, let the agent close a ticket and notify the customer without a human reviewer whenever the model's calibrated confidence exceeded a configurable threshold. The commercial logic was plain: Ankan's buyers are support-operations heads whose budget line is cost per contact, and a feature that removes a human from a third of tickets is the most saleable thing the company could ship in 2026. The disagreement was about what "worked" meant, and the disagreement was not rhetorical — it determined which events went into the specification and therefore which events would exist at all.

Menon's head of design argued for deflection rate: the proportion of tickets closed without human touch, an event trivially easy to emit at the moment of closure. Ankan's applied-science lead argued that deflection is an input, not an outcome, and that the only honest outcome event is ticket_reopened — a customer coming back on the same issue within nine days — which has the inconvenient property of arriving nine days late and, worse, of under-counting the failures that matter most, because a customer who is wrongly told "your refund has been processed" and does not come back has not been served; she has been lost. The account-management lead wanted customer satisfaction scores; the response rate on Ankan's embedded CSAT prompt is 11 percent and is, as everyone in the room knew, dominated by the furious and the delighted. Arjun's own position, stated at the end of a long hour, was that all three were proxies, that a proxy is not disqualified by being a proxy, and that the specification had to say which proxy governed which decision and what would be done when they disagreed. That sentence — which proxy governs which decision — is the thing this page is about, and it is the thing that separates a telemetry table from a telemetry requirement.

2The idea, its history, and the schools that disagree about it

A telemetry requirement is a clause of a product specification that defines, before implementation, an event contract: the set of discrete, timestamped records a feature must emit; for each record, the precise predicate under which it fires and the guarantee that it fires exactly once under that predicate; the properties carried on it, with types, permitted values, cardinality expectations and a privacy classification; the surface that emits it — device firmware, client application, or server — and the delivery guarantee of that surface; the identity and correlation keys that let it be joined to other records; its retention period and stated purpose; the named party accountable for its continued health; and the metric or decision it exists to serve. A telemetry requirement is not a metric target and not a dashboard. It is an interface definition, and the most useful mental shift a practitioner makes is to stop thinking of events as logs and start thinking of them as a published API with consumers who will break if it changes.

The word is borrowed. "Telemetering" enters English in the 1930s to describe the remote measurement of electrical generation and transmission; it acquires its modern connotation through mid-century aerospace, where the defining constraint is that the instrumented object is unreachable and the measurement is the only access you have. That constraint translates exactly. A feature running on 12.4 lakh appliances or inside 11.4 lakh monthly tickets is unreachable in the same operational sense: no one at Aamap can watch a household in Nanded decide whether to book a technician.

The software lineage runs through four distinct waves, and the schools of thought that disagree today are each the residue of one of them. The first wave was server log analysis and then page-view web analytics — Urchin in the late 1990s, Google Analytics from 2005 — in which the unit of measurement was a page and the owner was marketing. The second wave, roughly 2009 to 2013, moved the unit from the page to the user action: Mixpanel, KISSmetrics and Amplitude made it cheap for a product team to define arbitrary named events with arbitrary properties and to query funnels and retention over them, and the practice of writing a tracking plan before shipping emerged alongside them. Segment, founded in 2011, contributed the crucial abstraction that an event is emitted once and fanned out to many consumers, which forced the realisation that the event's shape is a contract with parties the emitting engineer has never met. Snowplow, from 2012, pushed this further into schema-first territory, with a registry of versioned JSON schemas and hard validation at ingest: an event that does not conform is quarantined rather than silently accepted. Parallel to all of this, Google's HEART framework (2010) supplied the discipline of deriving signals from goals rather than the reverse, and the Lean Analytics literature of 2013 supplied the countervailing discipline of parsimony.

The third wave came from the reliability side of the house and arrived in product vocabulary late. Distributed tracing — OpenTracing in 2016, OpenCensus alongside it, merged into OpenTelemetry in 2019 — treated a unit of work as a trace composed of nested spans, each carrying arbitrary attributes, and the observability movement associated with Honeycomb argued forcefully that pre-aggregated metrics answer only the questions you thought to ask, whereas wide, high-cardinality events (cardinality being the number of distinct values a property can take — two for platform, millions for user identifier) preserve the ability to ask questions you have not yet imagined. The fourth wave is regulatory and economic: the General Data Protection Regulation's purpose-limitation principle from 2018, Apple's App Tracking Transparency in 2021 collapsing third-party device graphs and pushing teams back onto first-party in-product telemetry, and in India the Digital Personal Data Protection Act, 2023, with its consent-manager architecture, purpose specification and erasure obligations, which makes "what do we log and for how long" a question with legal consequences rather than only storage costs.

Out of these waves come four positions that competent, experienced practitioners genuinely hold, and that differ not in emphasis but in the propositions they will sign.

The argument between the question-first and wide-event schools is the live one, and it is worth stating at its sharpest because both protagonists sit on its horns. The question-first position holds that an unbounded event surface is not free: every property is a maintenance obligation, a privacy exposure and a source of ambiguity, and a catalogue of 400 events with no owner is functionally equivalent to no catalogue at all, because analysts stop trusting any of it. The wide-event position holds that the expensive mistake is not over-collection but under-collection, because you can always ignore a property you captured and you can never retrieve one you did not, and the specific moment at which you discover you needed a property is the moment you are under maximum time pressure. Devyani's fleet constraint makes the second position physically impossible on 38 percent of her units and therefore forces the first. Arjun's problem — a model whose failure modes he demonstrably cannot enumerate in advance, since the whole premise of the feature is that it generalises to tickets nobody anticipated — pushes hard towards the second. Neither is universally right, and the practitioner's skill is knowing which constraint binds.

3Mechanics in depth: the contract, the pipeline, and where the truth leaks

Expert practice begins not with an event list but with a decision statement of a specific grammar: by date D, we will choose between action A and action B, on the basis of quantity Q measured over population P, and we will choose A if Q exceeds threshold T. Devyani's is: by 30 April, we will either make Predictive Filter Alert the default for all service-plan units or revert to the calendar reminder, on the basis of the on-time replacement rate — a filter replacement booked and completed within 21 days of predicted exhaustion — measured over service-plan households whose filter came due during the test window, and we will roll it out if the alert arm exceeds the calendar arm by at least two percentage points. Every element of that sentence generates a requirement. "Booked and completed" names two events, not one. "Within 21 days of predicted exhaustion" fixes the window origin at a system-computed timestamp, which must itself be emitted or the window cannot be reconstructed. "Service-plan households" defines a population that must be resolvable from a join key present on the event. "By 30 April" sets a deadline that interacts, as we will see, with telemetry latency in a way that nearly destroyed the experiment.

The second step is choosing the emitting surface, and this is where most specifications are silently wrong. Any given fact can usually be emitted from more than one place, and the choice determines the fidelity. A client — a mobile app, a browser, appliance firmware — knows things the server cannot: that a screen was rendered, that a notification tray was opened, that a user hesitated. But a client emits into an unreliable channel through a local buffer that may never flush, on a device whose clock may be wrong, under an operating system that may terminate the process. A server knows only what reached it, but what reached it, it knows with the reliability of its own database. The operative rule among experienced practitioners is blunt: any event that a finance, compliance or legal function will ever have to reconcile must be emitted server-side, from the same transaction that changed the state. Money moved, a loan disbursed, a ticket closed, a service booking created — these are state transitions, and a state transition already has an authoritative record; the telemetry requirement should say "derive this event from the state-transition log," not "have the app fire an event when the confirmation screen appears."

The third step is the event contract itself, and the properties that matter are rarely the interesting-sounding ones. Every event needs an idempotency key: a value that is stable across retries so that at-least-once delivery does not become at-least-once counting. Every event needs correlation keys naming the entities it belongs to — for Aamap a device serial, a household account and a service-cycle identifier; for Ankan a ticket identifier, a buyer account and a conversation thread — chosen before the properties, because a property you forgot can sometimes be reconstructed from an adjacent system and a missing join key usually cannot. Every event needs a schema version, and every property needs a privacy class, a purpose and a retention period, because under the DPDP Act a request to erase a data principal's records has to be executable against the event store, and a team that has never asked "can we delete one household from four years of appliance telemetry" will discover the answer during an audit rather than during design.

The fourth step, almost always left implicit, is the specification of failure and absence. Competent teams enumerate the happy path. Experts enumerate the sad paths as first-class events with reason codes — booking_failed with reason ∈ {no_slot, pincode_unserved, payment_declined, user_cancelled} — and then specify the absence condition: the derived event, computed downstream, that marks a unit as having entered the funnel and not emerged within the window. Absence is where product problems live, and absence cannot be observed directly; it must be constructed, which means the entry event and the window origin must both be present and both be trustworthy. Aamap's entry event is filter_exhaustion_predicted, emitted server-side by the prediction service rather than by the appliance, precisely so that the denominator exists even for households whose appliance goes offline the following day.

Two things about Table 2 repay attention. First, five of the eight events are server-emitted, including both numerators, and the one client-side event is explicitly labelled as available on 4.x only and as measuring attention rather than outcome. Devyani's team arrived at this arrangement after her operations manager's objection: by moving the decisive events to the service backend, the experiment became measurable across the whole fleet, including 3.x units and including households who book by calling the call centre, which is 31 percent of bookings and would have been invisible to any app-centric event scheme. Second, usage_rollup_15m is a hundred times larger than everything else combined and serves none of the launch decision. The original firmware proposal was a reading every sixty seconds: 12.4 lakh units × 1,440 readings = 178.6 crore events a day, which at Aamap's ingestion pricing of roughly ₹0.90 per lakh events would have cost about ₹16 lakh a day, or ₹58 crore a year, to measure a business worth ₹190 crore. Aggregating at the edge to a fifteen-minute rollup and restricting continuous telemetry to service-plan units brought that to 4.71 crore events a day and about ₹1.5 crore a year — still the largest line in the data budget, and justified only because it feeds model retraining, not because anyone looks at it.

The quantitative treatment that experts actually run has two halves, and teams reliably do the first and skip the second. The first is statistical power. For a two-arm comparison of proportions at 95 percent confidence and 80 percent power, a serviceable approximation is n ≈ 16 · p(1−p) / δ², where p is the baseline rate and δ the difference worth detecting. Aamap's baseline on-time replacement rate is 62 percent and the threshold for action is three percentage points, giving n ≈ 16 × 0.62 × 0.38 / 0.0009 ≈ 4,190 cycles per arm. With roughly 49,000 service-plan cycles coming due each month, that is reached in about six days of exposure, and a naïve reading of this arithmetic produces the confident statement that the experiment can be read in a week. The second half is what destroys that statement: the outcome is defined over a 21-day window, so the last cycle enrolled on day six cannot be evaluated until day twenty-seven, and the telemetry itself arrives late. It is the interaction of these two — outcome latency and telemetry latency — that produces the near-miss described below, and it is the second-order effect that no sample-size calculator surfaces.

4When the practice applies, and when it actively misleads

The conditions under which a telemetry requirement can carry a launch decision are worth stating as four testable claims, each of which can be checked before a line of instrumentation is written, and each of which fails for at least one of our protagonists.

Claim one: the success of the feature is expressible as a change in the rate of an observable action within a bounded window. For Aamap this holds cleanly — a replacement completed within 21 days of a system-generated predicted date is observable, bounded and unambiguous. For Ankan it holds only partially. "Ticket resolved correctly" is not observable; a closed ticket is observable, a reopened ticket is observable, a satisfaction score is observable-when-volunteered. The gap between the construct and anything emitted is the central fact of Arjun's problem, and a specification that pretends otherwise by defining success as deflection rate has not solved the measurement problem, it has redefined the goal to match the available instrument.

Claim two: the volume of that action within the decision horizon is sufficient to distinguish a difference worth acting on from noise. Aamap passes at the cycle level. Ankan passes overwhelmingly at the ticket level — 11.4 lakh a month makes even a half-point difference detectable within days — and fails absolutely at the level that determines the company's fate, which is accounts. With 64 accounts and an annual churn of perhaps four or five, no telemetry scheme, however elegant, will ever establish a statistical relationship between Autonomous Resolve and renewal. Arjun's temptation, and it is a general one, is to let the instrument's precision at the ticket level substitute for evidence at the account level. Mature practice here is to say so explicitly in the specification: this event set governs the ship/no-ship decision and does not govern the renewal question, which will be assessed qualitatively through structured account reviews.

Claim three: the emitting surface is under your control and updatable on the decision horizon. This is where Aamap's 3.x fleet bites, and it bites in a specific and instructive way. It is not merely that 38 percent of units cannot emit rich events; it is that the un-instrumentable 38 percent is systematically different from the instrumentable 62 percent — older, more rural, with worse connectivity and, per Aamap's own service records, a baseline on-time replacement rate of 54 percent against the 4.x fleet's 67 percent. Instrumenting only what is easy to instrument does not give you a noisy estimate of the truth; it gives you a precise estimate of a different population. The countermeasure Devyani adopted — routing the decisive events through the service backend, which sees every fleet generation equally — is the general form of the answer: when the client population is not representative, move the measurement to a surface whose coverage is.

Claim four: measuring does not change what is measured, and you are permitted to measure it. For Ankan this fails on the second half in a way that took the legal team three weeks to unpick. The thing that would most convincingly prove Autonomous Resolve worked is the full text of the ticket and the agent's reply, judged by a competent human. That text is the buyer's customer data, processed by Ankan as a processor under contracts that in several cases forbid retention beyond the operational window. Ankan can log the ticket identifier, the intent classification, the tool calls, the model version, the confidence and the outcome; it cannot freely retain the content on which a quality judgement depends. The specification therefore had to invent a mechanism — a consented, time-boxed audit sample under a separate data-processing addendum, covering roughly 300 tickets a week — rather than assume the evidence was available for the asking.

There is also a class of situation in which the practice is not merely inapplicable but actively misleading, and it deserves naming because it looks like good practice while it does its damage. When the enumerated events become the operative definition of success, every harm that falls outside the enumeration becomes invisible and is thereby treated as absent. A customer wrongly told her refund was processed, who does not reopen and does not answer the survey and quietly stops buying, appears in Ankan's telemetry as a clean autonomous resolution with no reopen and no complaint — the best possible record. This is not an argument against instrumentation; it is an argument for including at least one measurement channel whose construction does not depend on the user taking an action, which in Ankan's case is the human audit sample and in Aamap's case is the churn analysis run against the service ledger six months later. An event system measures what people did. It is structurally blind to what they silently stopped doing.

5Hard edge cases and the organisational seams

Two-sided and platform situations. In a marketplace, the unit of success is a match, and a match is a fact about two parties that neither party's client can observe. The requirement is not "instrument both sides" but "specify the join": a transaction identifier minted at the earliest possible moment and threaded through every subsequent event on both sides, with an explicit statement of which side's event is authoritative when they disagree. The failure mode is subtle — demand-side and supply-side events instrumented by two teams with two naming conventions and no shared key, producing two internally consistent funnels that cannot be composed. In platform situations the same problem appears across the first-party/third-party boundary: when a partner's application emits events into your pipeline, you have acquired a producer you cannot review, and the mature answer is a validated ingestion contract with quarantine and a partner-facing conformance report, not trust.

Hardware plus software. Aamap's situation generalises badly, which is the point. A software team can change what it emits weekly; a firmware fleet updates on a schedule measured in quarters and never reaches everyone. Three consequences follow. First, event schemas on device must be designed for forward compatibility from the outset — fixed-width, additive, with reserved fields — because you will be reading events from a schema you wrote three years ago for the rest of the product's life. Second, the fleet's schema-version distribution becomes a permanent property of every analysis: at Aamap, any trend line spanning 2023 to 2026 is partly a measurement of fleet composition, not behaviour. Third, telemetry has a marginal cost per byte when the transport is cellular, which converts an engineering aesthetic question into a finance question and forces edge aggregation of exactly the sort described above.

Regulated products. In lending, insurance, health and payments, the specification acquires a second reader. The Reserve Bank of India's guidelines on digital lending, the DPDP Act's purpose-limitation and erasure provisions, and sectoral data-localisation expectations mean that a property is not merely a column; it is a processing activity that must have a stated purpose, a lawful basis and a retention period. Practitioners in these sectors write the privacy classification into the event contract as a required field, and the discipline pays an unexpected dividend: forcing a purpose statement per property is the single most effective way of deleting properties nobody can justify.

AI-native products. Ankan's case is the general case, and it differs from conventional instrumentation in four ways. The output is non-deterministic, so an event must carry the generative context — model version, prompt or policy version, retrieval set identifier, tool calls made, calibrated confidence — or a later analyst cannot tell whether a change in outcome reflects a change in users or a silent change in the model. The quality of the output is not observable at emission time; it is judged later, by a human or by a downstream consequence, which means the architecture must support late binding of the outcome to the event, typically by writing a judgement record keyed to the original interaction rather than by mutating it. Implicit feedback becomes a first-class signal: where a human reviewer edits the agent's draft before sending, the edit distance between draft and sent text is a continuous, unprompted quality measure worth more than any survey. And the system is a moving target: an event set specified against one model generation loses meaning when the model is replaced, so the specification must version the interpretation as well as the schema.

The organisational seams, and what mature companies actually do. The published version of telemetry governance at large companies describes a schema registry, a review board and continuous-integration tests that fail a build when a contracted event stops firing. The lived version is messier in three specific places. The first seam is the vendor boundary: notification delivery, payments and customer messaging are frequently third-party, which means the event that proves your feature worked is emitted by a system whose schema you do not control and whose backfills arrive on their schedule. The second is acquisition: an acquired product arrives with its own taxonomy, and the honest practice at mature companies is not migration but a mapping layer plus an explicit statement of which cross-product questions cannot be answered, maintained for years. The third is the platform team's incentive: a central data-platform group is measured on pipeline reliability and cost, not on whether a product team can answer its question, so proposals that increase volume meet resistance that is rational for the platform and irrational for the firm. Companies that handle this well give product teams a telemetry budget denominated in events per day and cardinality, and let them spend it — which converts an argument about virtue into an allocation decision, and is the single most effective governance intervention this author has seen described.

6The nuances that separate an expert from a competent practitioner

One: the expert specifies absence and failure before success. A competent specification enumerates the happy path and adds a generic error event. An expert writes the reason-coded failure events first, on the reasoning that the happy path will be instrumented anyway — someone always wants the conversion number — whereas nobody lobbies for booking_failed until the day it is needed. The tell-tale sign in the wild is a funnel chart in which the gap between two stages is large and entirely uninterpretable: the team can see that 1,840 cycles lapsed but cannot say how many lapsed because no slot was available in that pincode. The obvious reading — "we can dig into that later" — is wrong, because the diagnostic properties would have to have been attached at the moment of failure and there is no later.

Two: the expert knows which events must be server-emitted and does not negotiate. The rule is that any quantity that a second function will independently compute must originate from the authoritative state transition. The tell-tale sign is a persistent, stable discrepancy of two to five percent between the product dashboard and the finance or operations system, which teams learn to explain away with the phrase "there's always some drift." There is not always some drift; there is a specific mechanism producing a specific bias, and the bias is almost never random, because the devices and network conditions that drop events are correlated with the users you care most about. The obvious reading — client events are closer to the user and therefore truer — inverts the actual reliability ordering.

Three: the expert treats an event name as an immutable public interface. Changing what an existing event means, while keeping its name, is the most destructive single act available to a product team, because every dashboard, alert, cohort definition and model feature built on that name silently changes meaning and nothing errors. The tell-tale sign is a sentence in a design review: "we'll just repurpose that event, nobody's using it for much." The expert's response is additive — a new name, or a new schema version with the old one maintained through a deprecation window — and the obvious objection, that this proliferates events, is answered by observing that a deprecated event with a retirement date is a smaller problem than a trusted event that lies.

Four: the expert specifies identity and correlation keys before properties. Properties describe; keys connect, and analysis is almost entirely connection. The classic wound is the anonymous-to-identified transition: a user browses anonymously under a device identifier, then signs in, and unless an aliasing record links the two, the pre-login funnel and the post-login funnel cannot be composed, producing either a conversion rate that is impossibly low or a user count that is inflated by a factor the team never quite pins down. The tell-tale sign is a monthly-active-user figure that exceeds a plausible estimate of the customer base. The obvious reading — that identity is a platform concern — is wrong because the decision about when to alias, and what to do with events emitted before the alias, is a product decision with visible consequences for every metric.

Five: the expert declares which clock the metric uses. An event carries at least three times: when the emitting surface believes it happened, when the gateway received it, and when the warehouse materialised it. Ordering a funnel by device clock across a population where a meaningful fraction of devices have skewed clocks produces impossible sequences — a payment completing before it started — while counting daily volume by receipt time makes a connectivity outage look like a behaviour change. The tell-tale sign is a chart whose recent days keep moving upward for a week after the fact and a team that has learned to "ignore the last few days." The obvious reading is that this is a cosmetic annoyance; it is not, because whether the last few days are ignorable depends entirely on whether the lateness is equally distributed across the arms of the comparison being made, and it usually is not.

Six: the expert instruments the counterfactual. A specification that describes only what the new experience emits leaves the comparison arm invisible, and a team then finds itself comparing a richly instrumented treatment against an inferred control. The discipline is to ensure that the control path emits the same decisive events under the same definitions — which frequently means retrofitting instrumentation onto the old flow before shipping the new one, an expenditure that feels wasteful and is the precondition for the experiment meaning anything. The tell-tale sign is a launch review in which the treatment's funnel has six stages and the control's has two.

Seven: the expert budgets telemetry in volume, cardinality and rupees. Free-text properties are the specific hazard. At Aamap an early build attached a device-generated error_detail string to fault events; because the string embedded a serial number and a sensor reading, distinct values reached 2.14 lakh within a month, and a single grouped query over three months of that column cost more than a fortnight of the entire ingestion bill. The tell-tale sign is a warehouse cost line growing faster than usage. The obvious reading — that storage is cheap — is true of storage and false of cardinality, which drives index size, shuffle volume and query cost super-linearly.

Eight: the expert writes purpose and retention per property, not per system. Under a consent-and-purpose regime, "we retain analytics data for 24 months" is not a policy, it is an aspiration; the operative question is whether a particular property has a purpose that survives scrutiny and whether an erasure request can reach it. The tell-tale sign is an inability to answer, within a day, how many distinct tables contain a given identifier. The obvious reading — that this is legal's problem — is wrong in the specific sense that the cheapest moment to reduce the exposure is the moment before the property is written into the contract, and the most expensive moment is every moment thereafter.

Nine: the expert validates the dashboard against synthetic events before code freeze. The practice is simple: generate the events the contract describes, at plausible volumes and with plausible distributions including malformed ones, and confirm that every chart the launch decision depends on renders correctly and produces the expected numbers. The tell-tale sign of its absence is the discovery, on launch day, that a chart is empty for a reason nobody can diagnose under pressure. The obvious objection — that this tests nothing real — misses the point: it does not test the feature, it tests the measurement apparatus, and the measurement apparatus is the thing whose failure is silent.

Ten: the expert knows when not to instrument. An enterprise feature used by seven named accounts does not have a measurement problem; it has a conversation problem, and a beautifully specified event contract over seven accounts produces numbers whose confidence intervals span the entire decision space while consuming the engineering week that could have bought three customer visits. The tell-tale sign is a specification whose telemetry section is longer than its functional section for a feature with a three-figure addressable population. The obvious reading — that rigour is always virtuous — confuses the form of evidence with its weight.

7How the practice differs by product type and company stage

Across consumer, B2B and enterprise the difference is real and it is a difference of unit and of n. Consumer telemetry is keyed to a person or an install, volumes make almost any question answerable within days, and the binding constraints are cost, privacy and the representativeness of the instrumented population. B2B telemetry is keyed to an account and a seat, and the decisive questions — is this account adopting, is it at risk — are account-level questions with an n in the hundreds, which means telemetry supports judgement rather than replacing it; the practical consequence is that B2B event contracts almost always require an account identifier on every event and are reviewed jointly with customer success. Enterprise telemetry adds a third party with veto power: the buyer may contractually restrict what may be collected from their users, may require on-premises processing, and may demand their own copy, so the specification acquires a "what the customer sees" column. Platform and marketplace products differ from all three in that the unit of success is a relationship rather than an action, which makes the join key, not the event list, the object of design.

Hardware and physical goods differ in kind rather than degree, for the reasons set out above: a schema you cannot update, a fleet that never fully converges, a marginal cost per byte, and — the point most easily missed — the fact that the physical outcome frequently occurs outside any instrumented system. Aamap can observe that a technician closed a job and scanned a part serial; it cannot observe whether the household's water quality improved, and the temptation to treat the scan as the outcome rather than the proxy is exactly the temptation Arjun faces with deflection. AI products differ for the reasons in Section 5, and the honest statement is that the field has not settled how to specify telemetry for a system whose behaviour changes when the model changes; what has settled is that the generative context must be on the event.

By stage, the difference is less profound than the literature suggests, and it is worth saying plainly where it is not real. The question — what events will prove this worked — is identical at ten people and ten thousand. What changes is the apparatus. At seed and Series A stage the telemetry requirement is a table in the specification, the PM adds events directly in an analytics tool, and the entire catalogue fits in one person's head; the failure mode is not writing it down at all, and the correct amount of governance is approximately none. At growth stage the failure mode inverts: multiple teams emit into a shared namespace, event names collide, and nobody owns the catalogue, which is where a registry and a naming convention start to pay for themselves. At scale the apparatus becomes a schema registry with enforced validation, contract tests in continuous integration that fail a build if a contracted event disappears, volume alerting routed to named owners, a deprecation process and a cost allocation model. What does not change with stage — and what the largest companies get wrong at least as often as the smallest — is the choice of which event represents success, because that is a judgement about the product's purpose and no amount of platform machinery supplies it.

8Three worked examples, including one that failed

Example one: Aamap and the experiment that was nearly read four weeks early

Predictive Filter Alert entered a controlled rollout on 2 March 2026 with a 50/50 split of service-plan cycles coming due, evaluated on filter_replaced within 21 days of filter_exhaustion_predicted. By 2 April, 4,188 cycles per arm had completed their windows, satisfying the power requirement. Devyani's analyst pulled the numbers on the morning of 3 April and found the alert arm at 52.9 percent against the calendar arm at 58.1 percent — a five-point loss, comfortably outside any plausible noise band, and a result that would have killed the feature that afternoon had the review not been scheduled for the following week.

What had happened was differential telemetry latency. The filter_replaced event originates in a technician's handheld application, which syncs when it finds connectivity; technicians serving dense metro routes sync several times a day, while those working tier-three towns and rural routes often sync at the end of a multi-day circuit. The alert arm, by design, reached more low-connectivity households — that was the point of routing alerts through the device LED on 3.x units — and therefore its completions were served disproportionately by the slower-syncing technicians. Both arms were under-counted; the alert arm was under-counted much more.

10Where experts genuinely disagree

Enumerate narrowly, or capture widely? The narrow position, steelmanned: every event is a liability with a maintenance cost, a privacy surface and an interpretive ambiguity, and catalogues grow monotonically because nothing is ever deleted; the evidence is the observable state of large event catalogues, where a substantial majority of registered events have no consumer and analysts routinely cannot determine which of four similarly named events is correct. It would have to be true, for this position to be wrong, that the cost of an unused event is genuinely near zero and that analysts can reliably navigate a large catalogue — which is an argument about tooling, and tooling has improved. The wide position, steelmanned: the questions that matter most are the ones nobody anticipated, and a decision taken with the wrong data because the right property was never captured costs more than every unused column combined; the evidence is the repeated experience of incident analysis, where the property that explains a failure is almost never the one someone thought to specify. It would have to be true, for this position to be wrong, that the marginal insight from breadth is small — which is more plausible for mature, well-understood products than for novel ones, and that conditionality is the real resolution nobody states cleanly.

Should the product manager specify events at all? The warehouse-first position holds that a specification should carry the decision and the metric's definition, and that naming event properties is over-specification that couples a product document to an implementation that will change; the evidence is the number of specifications carrying event names that were never implemented as written, and the observation that downstream modelling can usually reconstruct a metric from whatever was captured. The opposing position holds that "usually reconstruct" conceals the crucial case: you can reconstruct from a richer substrate, and you cannot conjure a substrate that was never emitted; the moment of leverage is the moment the emitting code is written, and the only document in the room at that moment is the specification. This disagreement is not resolvable in the abstract because it turns on whether the organisation's default capture is generous or stingy, which varies enormously.

Is a proxy with fast feedback better than a true measure with slow feedback? The velocity position holds that a decision loop of two days with a 70 percent correlated proxy beats a loop of three weeks with the real thing, because the faster loop takes more decisions and compounds; this is the reasoning behind the industry's attachment to leading indicators, and it has serious empirical support in fast-iterating consumer products. The integrity position holds that proxies drift under optimisation pressure — that the act of managing to a proxy is precisely what destroys its correlation with the goal, a mechanism general enough to have a name — and that the compounding is therefore compounding in the wrong direction. Arjun sits exactly on this fault line: deflection rate is fast and correlated; optimise it and the correlation degrades, because the easiest way to raise deflection is to lower the threshold. What would have to be true for the velocity position to hold is that the proxy is monitored against the true measure frequently enough to detect drift before it matters — which is an argument for keeping both, at different cadences, and is close to what mature teams actually do without articulating it.

Who owns the event catalogue? The federated position holds that teams own their events, because ownership follows the ability to fix, and central registries become bottlenecks that teams route around. The central position holds that events are a shared asset whose value is entirely in their consistency, and that federation reliably produces four incompatible definitions of "active user"; the evidence is that every large company that federated has subsequently built a central taxonomy function. Neither side disputes the other's evidence; they weigh cost of delay against cost of inconsistency differently, and the honest statement is that the correct answer depends on whether your most expensive recent mistake was a slow decision or a wrong one.

11What mastery looks like

Someone who has merely studied this writes a good telemetry table. Someone who has internalised it behaves differently in four observable ways. First, they start from the decision and its date, not from the feature, and they will decline to specify events until someone states what will be chosen between and when — which often reveals that the team does not actually have a decision, only a wish to appear rigorous. Second, they interrogate the emitting surface before the event list, asking of every proposed event where it will be emitted from, what fraction of the affected population that surface covers, and how the covered fraction differs from the uncovered one; this single habit would have prevented the Aakalan reversal and shaped Aamap's contract. Third, they specify the failure paths, the absence conditions and the watermark as a matter of course, and they treat "we'll look into that later" as an error rather than a deferral, because they have learned that the diagnostic properties must be attached at the moment of the failure. Fourth, and most distinctively, they hold the enumerated events lightly: they know that the event set is a model of what matters, that a model omits, and that the omissions are where the unpleasant surprises live — so they insist on at least one measurement channel that does not depend on a user taking an action, and they are the person in the review who asks what a customer who was badly served and said nothing would look like in this data. They are also, in the same breath, willing to say that a feature serving nine accounts does not need any of this. Mastery here is not maximal rigour; it is the accurate placement of rigour.

12The decisions, and questions for discussion

Devyani Rao's specification, signed on 17 February, did three things. It moved every decisive event to the service backend, making the experiment measurable across both firmware generations and across the 31 percent of bookings that arrive through the call centre, and relegated the 4.x client events to a clearly labelled secondary role measuring attention rather than outcome. It set a watermark of nine days on filter_replaced and forbade the reporting of the primary metric before it, with the arrival curve attached whenever a provisional figure was shared — the clause that, six weeks later, kept a five-point apparent loss from becoming a cancellation. And it cut the firmware telemetry proposal from a sixty-second reading to a fifteen-minute edge rollup, restricted to service-plan units, on the explicit ground that the high-volume stream served model retraining and not the launch decision, and should therefore be budgeted against the model's value rather than the feature's. Her reasoning, stated in the specification's preamble, was that the population she could measure had to match the population she was trying to help, and that everything else was negotiable.

Arjun Menon shipped Autonomous Resolve on 4 March at a confidence threshold of 0.92 rather than the 0.86 the cost model favoured, accepting ₹50 lakh a month of forgone gross saving in exchange for a reduction in audited wrong-closes from four percent to 1.9 percent. He wrote two unusual clauses into the specification. The first made the weekly 300-ticket human audit a funded, staffed component of the feature rather than a research activity, with a named owner and a service level, on the reasoning that the only rung of the evidence ladder that measures quality cannot be the only one that is optional. The second was a reporting rule: deflection rate may not appear in any internal or customer-facing document without the audited wrong-close rate on the same page, for the same period. He conceded in the review that 0.92 might be too conservative and that he expected to raise it once the audit series was long enough to establish where the curve bent; what he was unwilling to do was raise it on the strength of the only number that was free to collect.

  1. Devyani's solution to the 3.x fleet problem was to move measurement to a surface with complete coverage. Suppose that option had not existed — that the only record of a filter replacement was a technician's handheld sync. What experimental design, if any, would have let her reach a defensible conclusion, and what would she have had to give up to get it?
  2. Arjun's audit sample is 300 tickets a week against 11.4 lakh a month. At that ratio, how large a change in wrong-close rate could he detect within a quarter, and does the answer change your view of whether 0.92 was the right threshold or merely the cautious one? What would you fund differently?
  3. Aakalan Money's rollback followed a pre-registered criterion applied honestly to a precisely measured number. If disciplined process produced the wrong answer, what should Aakalan add to its process — and at what point does the addition cost more than the error it prevents?

13Going deeper

PRD structure. Telemetry is a requirement with the same standing as a functional one, and where it sits in the document determines whether it is reviewed or skimmed; understanding the anatomy of the specification is what lets you place the event contract where engineering and data both have to sign it.

Designing an event taxonomy. The contract in this page selects names from a shared vocabulary; a weak taxonomy makes even a perfect telemetry table unusable by anyone outside the team, and this is the topic that turns individual discipline into organisational capability.

PM artefacts: one-pager, PRD, spec, strategy doc. Knowing which artefact carries which commitment tells you where a telemetry requirement belongs at each stage of a decision — a one-pager states the question, a specification states the contract, and confusing the two produces either premature precision or unenforceable intent.

Writing a one-pager. The decision statement described in Section 3 — choose between A and B by date D on quantity Q — is the spine of a good one-pager, and drafting it well upstream is what makes the event list downstream nearly mechanical.

Customer narratives (Day 0 / Day N). Walking a customer's first day and hundredth day is the most reliable way to discover the events you would otherwise omit, particularly the absence conditions, because the Day N narrative is where silent abandonment becomes visible as a story before it is visible as a metric.

Acceptance criteria and error cases. Reason-coded failure events are acceptance criteria wearing different clothes; teams that write rigorous error cases usually discover they have already written half their telemetry contract, and the two documents should be drafted together.

Non-functional requirements. Delivery guarantees, latency, retention, cardinality budgets and privacy classification are non-functional requirements of the telemetry system itself, and treating them as such is what stops a specification from promising evidence the pipeline cannot deliver.

Release criteria and success metrics. This is where the loop closes: a release criterion that names a metric whose constituent events are in the contract, with a stated watermark, is enforceable; one that names a number is a wish. Read next, it converts everything on this page into a gate.

Inaiyam Systems: Proving Reorder Assist

Inaiyam Systems and Iqleem Retail Group are fictional. Indian brands and statutes named here are real market context.

1. Thursday night

At a quarter to eleven on Thursday, 12 November 2026, Ramitha Bhuvanagiri was still at her desk in the building Inaiyam Systems rents off Old Madras Road in Bengaluru. Diwali week had emptied the floor, and the rain came sideways across the glass.

Three things were open in front of her. A spreadsheet from her data scientist in Toronto, sent on 2 November: twenty-seven days of event data from 1,478 rep handsets — the first figures Inaiyam had held that tied a tap on a suggested item to an order line. An attribution audit, circulated three days later, reporting the same feature's effect in rupees from no client event at all. And the requirements document she had signed on 14 March 2025, whose Success metrics section promised five per cent more lines per invoice while no section named an event.

On Monday, 16 November, the steering group wanted a decision; on Wednesday the 25th, the board wanted a number. On 31 March 2027 the Iqleem Retail Group renewal fell due, with twelve per cent of a ₹18.4 crore annual fee — ₹2.21 crore — against an uplift measured on visits where Reorder Assist is active.

2. The company, and a promise made in 2019

Rameshan Balaganapathy and two colleagues founded Inaiyam Systems in Bengaluru in 2016 to build retail execution software: an Android application, Inaiyam Field, that a distributor's salesman carries from outlet to outlet with the beat plan, the price list and the order pad. Its customers are the distributors who put Dabur, Marico, Britannia and Amul lines onto shelves in Erode and Jalandhar. FY26 revenue was ₹138 crore against an FY27 plan of ₹171 crore; on 31 October 2026 the platform carried 1,164 tenants and 58,400 active rep handsets.

One 2019 decision shapes what Ramitha can now do. To close a Nagpur distribution group with 2,100 reps that November, Inaiyam agreed that the client's own device management console would pin the application version, and that upgrades would move on a calendar the client controlled. Sales reused the clause; by October 2026 it covered 41 tenants and 28,900 handsets, or 49.5 per cent of the installed base.

3. The industry

Indian retail execution software is crowded and price-led; the industry Zoho and Freshworks made legible to global buyers also made its margins visible to every procurement team. Cheap mobile data made an always-syncing field application viable on a ₹7,000 handset, which is most of Inaiyam's fleet: entry-level Android, four generations of it.

Regulation enters at two points. The order log is a book of account for goods and services tax, and Inaiyam keeps it seven years; GST e-invoicing forces a compliance release most quarters. The Digital Personal Data Protection Act, 2023 governs the notice and consent under which Inaiyam processes a rep's data for the distributor, making new client-side collection a papering exercise as much as an engineering one. Outside India, the Gulf and South-East Asia produced ₹33.1 crore of FY26 revenue, 24 per cent, more than half through Iqleem Retail Group of Dubai, which runs 1,180 reps in the UAE, Oman and Qatar.

4. What was believed, and what has since turned out otherwise

Reorder Assist was conceived in January 2025 (Figure 1). When a rep opens the order screen at an outlet, the application shows up to five suggested items from a nightly recommendation file; the rep taps a chip to add one. The PRD was signed on 14 March 2025 targeting five per cent more lines per invoice. A separate two-page document, the analytics ask, listed eleven events, among them a shown event carrying slot, item code and model version, an accepted event and a dismissal with a reason.

On 23 May 2025, in the last sprint before release, the analytics ask was descoped; the sprint note records it in one line — reuse existing screen_view / tap; analytics to be added post-GA — and states the belief that the order log would suffice, since it held every line of every invoice. Reorder Assist went live to 64 tenants on 15 August 2025.

In November 2025 Iqleem signed an expansion putting twelve per cent of its annual fee against a contracted uplift of six per cent in lines per invoice on visits where Reorder Assist is active, evidenced by system-generated reports; the deal memo recorded the belief that lines per invoice was already measured. On 19 February 2026 the board heard that Reorder Assist tenants had gained 11.4 per cent over the nine months to December 2025 against 2.9 per cent elsewhere, on a slide with no denominators and from an extract that was not retained.

Four things have since come out. A taxonomy review on 28 October 2026 found that up to version 4.1 the suggestion chip emitted tap with the identifier chip_add_sku, as did three other add-to-order controls on the same screen. A tenant-size audit on 20 October put the earliest-enabled cohort's median rep count at 96 against 19 for tenants that never enabled it. Iqleem's fleet, pinned at version 4.1, emits no suggestion events. And Iqleem introduced a new trade-promotion scheme across its UAE territories in May 2026, inside H1 FY27.

5. The people

Ramitha Bhuvanagiri, Vice-President, Product, Bengaluru, signed the March 2025 PRD and chaired the sprint review that dropped the analytics ask. She holds that the instrument must be fixed before the number is defended; her FY27 objectives carry the three Q4 features and no rebuild. She has told nobody she cannot remember whether the descope was a deferral or a cancellation.

Rameshan Balaganapathy, co-founder and chief executive, Bengaluru, wants a defensible figure for the 25 November board, which seats two institutional investors and opens a Series D conversation in January. Telemetry Requirements

What events must a feature emit so that, weeks after launch, someone can prove — not argue, prove — whether it worked?

On the morning of 11 March 2026, Ritika Sarin, senior product manager at Charuta Health, a Mumbai-based teleconsultation and chronic-care app with just over four million installs, opened the dashboard for the Teleconsult Booking Redesign and found it exactly as empty as it had been the day before. The redesign had shipped six weeks earlier: a simplified three-step booking flow meant to lift completed bookings by an estimated 12 to 15 percent, a number her VP had already mentioned to the board. Instead, week-four data from the app stores showed one-star reviews mentioning a "confusing new booking screen," and the weekly bookings count — the one number finance actually tracked — had fallen 18 percent. Nobody could say why. The new flow had never been instrumented beyond a generic screen_viewed event that fired for every screen in the app indiscriminately, so there was no way to see where inside the new three steps users were giving up, whether it was the date picker, the doctor-selection card, or the payment step. Ritika's data analyst, Faisal Rahman, spent eleven days reconstructing a rough funnel from support-ticket transcripts and a sample of screen recordings, because the one thing the team had not asked engineering to build was the one thing they needed most: a record of what users actually did, step by step, inside the feature they had just spent a quarter building.

By the time Faisal's reconstruction pointed to a payment-step bug affecting Android users on older OS versions, Charuta Health had already lost roughly three weeks of bookings to a competitor's app, and Ritika's VP of product, Anand Deshmukh, had lost patience. "I don't want a post-mortem next time," he told her in a one-on-one on 18 March. "I want the dashboard live the day the feature ships." Ritika's next assignment was Care Plan Adherence, a medication-reminder and symptom-check-in feature scheduled to launch in six weeks, aimed at Charuta's roughly 60,000 users managing hypertension and diabetes. This time, before a single screen was designed, Anand asked her to answer one question in the product requirements document itself, in writing, reviewed and signed off before development began: what events will this feature emit, and how will each one prove that it worked? That question — not "what will we build" but "what will we be able to see once we've built it" — is what this page is about.

The idea

Telemetry requirements are the part of a product specification that names, in advance, every event a feature must emit while a user interacts with it, together with the properties attached to each event and the metric each one is meant to feed. The word "telemetry" is borrowed from engineering and space flight, where it describes measurements taken at a remote, often inaccessible point and transmitted back to an observer who cannot see the thing directly — a rocket's fuel pressure radioed to a ground station, an aircraft engine's temperature streamed to a maintenance system. A product feature, once it is running on a few hundred thousand phones, is exactly that kind of remote, inaccessible thing: nobody at Charuta Health can stand behind a user's shoulder while she tries to book a teleconsultation, so the only way to know what happened is if the app itself reports it.

The practice of treating this reporting as a formal requirement — rather than an engineering afterthought bolted on once a feature already works — grew out of the product-analytics movement of the early-to-mid 2010s, when tools such as Mixpanel (founded 2009) and Amplitude (founded 2012) made it cheap for a product team, not just a data-engineering team, to define and query individual user events. Before that generation of tools, "analytics" mostly meant page-view counters run by a marketing or web-analytics function, disconnected from the people designing the product. What changed was the recognition, pushed hardest by growth-focused consumer companies in Silicon Valley and then absorbed into mainstream product management practice, that the events worth measuring are not generic (page viewed, button clicked) but specific to the job a feature is meant to do, and that naming them is a design decision, not an instrumentation detail — which is why the discipline now sits inside requirements and specification rather than inside data engineering. The single sentence Ritika could say in a meeting without sounding glib is this: if an event isn't in the spec, it won't be in the code, and if it isn't in the code, the feature's success or failure will be a matter of opinion.

How it actually works

Writing telemetry requirements is a sequence of decisions, and the order matters more than most teams assume. The first step is not "what should we log" but "what is the one thing this feature must cause a user to do, and by when, for us to call it a success." For Care Plan Adherence, Ritika and Anand agreed the feature's job was to get a user from installing a care plan to actually logging a dose taken — not merely opening the reminder screen, which tells you nothing about whether the medication was taken. That single sentence, written before any screens existed, became the anchor for everything that followed.

The second step is to walk the user's path end to end and name a distinct event at each point where the user makes a decision or the system does something on the user's behalf, then decide which of Charuta's existing taxonomy of event names each one maps onto — this is the direct link to designing an event taxonomy, the topic telemetry requirements draw on: a spec should never invent a new naming convention on the spot, it should select from, and where genuinely necessary extend, a shared vocabulary the whole company already uses, so that a data analyst two teams away can find "care plan created" without learning a new dialect. The third step is to attach properties to each event: not just that a plan was created, but which condition it was for, how many reminders were configured, and what plan identifier ties this event to the ones that will follow it downstream. The fourth step, the one practitioners most often skip, is to assign an owner to each event — a named person or team responsible for noticing if the event stops firing — and to decide, in the spec itself, which metric each event feeds, so the metric's definition is traceable back to a named event rather than existing only in someone's head.

What most teams leave implicit, and what Ritika made explicit for Care Plan Adherence, is the negative space around each event: an event needs a precise trigger condition (exactly what user action or system state causes it to fire, and exactly once), a precise timing rule (does "within 24 hours" mean 24 hours from install, from feature entry, or from account creation), and a precise absence condition — what does it mean, and what event or lack of one, indicates that a user tried and failed, as opposed to a user who never tried at all. Without that last piece, a team can count what happened but never see what should have happened and did not, which is usually where the real product problem lives.

A worked example

Ritika's team defined six events for Care Plan Adherence, shown in Table 1, each with a named owner and a stated destination metric — the direct answer to Anand's "prove it worked" instruction.

Consider what these events let the team compute once real data arrives. Say 10,000 users install Charuta Health in the first week after a marketing push tied to the launch. Of these, 6,400 open the app at least once — a 64 percent open rate. Of those 6,400 openers, 2,880 complete the onboarding wizard and tap "Save care plan" within 24 hours, which is 45 percent of openers, or 28.8 percent of all 10,000 installs (2,880 ÷ 10,000). Using careplan_created as the activation event — call this Definition A — Ritika can report an activation rate of 28.8 percent to Anand's leadership review.

But the team's stated job for the feature was never "get someone to save a plan" — it was "get someone to actually take a logged dose," because a saved plan with no logged doses has changed nothing about a patient's hypertension. So the team ran a second pass using medication_logged, fired within 72 hours of install, as the activation event instead — call this Definition B. Of the 2,880 users who created a plan, only 2,240 went on to log at least one dose within 72 hours of installing the app; the rest created a plan and then did nothing further inside that window, meaning the true care-relevant activation rate is 2,240 ÷ 10,000 = 22.4 percent, not 28.8 percent. That is a difference of 6.4 percentage points, a 22 percent relative overstatement if the team had reported Definition A to the board as if it were the real number. The gap between the two definitions — 640 users — is not noise; it is a specific, namable group: people who filled in a care plan and then never logged a single dose, which is precisely the population a medication-adherence feature exists to convert. Changing one input — which event counts as "activated" — changed the number leadership would see by nearly a quarter, and changed where Ritika's team looked next: not at onboarding completion, which was already fine, but at the 24-to-72-hour gap between saving a plan and logging a first dose, which turned out to be where most of the friction lived.

Why the second pass mattersDefinition A measures whether a form got submitted. Definition B measures whether the feature's actual job got done. A telemetry requirement is only as good as the event chosen to represent success — and that choice, made once, silently sets the ceiling on every metric the team will later trust.

The nuances a learner must become aware of

Telemetry is a requirement, not a chore appended to engineering's ticket. The most common failure mode, visible in the Teleconsult Booking Redesign, is treating instrumentation as something engineering does "if there's time," after the feature already works. Because telemetry requirements build directly on PRD structure, the discipline is to write the events section with the same authority as the functional requirements — a feature is not done when it works for a user, it is done when the team can prove, from data, whether it worked.

An event is not a metric. medication_logged is a fact — a single, timestamped thing that happened to one user. "Adherence rate" is arithmetic performed over a set of such facts across many users and a time window. Teams that confuse the two end up specifying metrics in the PRD ("we will hit 40 percent adherence") without ever naming the events that compose the denominator and numerator, which is how two dashboards later report two different numbers for what is nominally the same metric.

The proxy event is a choice, and the wrong choice is invisible until someone checks. Definition A and Definition B in the worked example were both defensible-sounding; only one of them matched what the feature was actually for. A thoughtful spec author asks, for every candidate activation event, "if a user did exactly this and nothing else, would I call the feature a success for them?" — and if the honest answer is no, that event is a proxy, not the real thing, and should be labelled as such in the PRD.

Telemetry cannot tell you why, only what and how many. Even a perfectly instrumented funnel will show that a user abandoned between careplan_created and medication_logged, but not whether she abandoned because the reminder time was wrong, because she distrusted the app with her medical schedule, or because she simply forgot the app existed. Quantitative telemetry narrows down where to look; it does not replace user interviews, support-ticket review, or usability testing, and a team that stops investigating once the funnel chart is built has mistaken measurement for understanding.

What gets logged is a privacy decision, not only a data-engineering one. Under India's Digital Personal Data Protection Act, 2023, health-adjacent data of the kind Charuta Health handles carries real consent and processing obligations; a property like condition_type attached to every event is personal health information travelling through a general-purpose analytics pipeline, and a telemetry spec that does not flag which properties are sensitive, and route them accordingly, is not merely sloppy — it can be non-compliant. This is commonly confused with generic "marketing tracking," which most product teams already know to be cautious about; the confusion is thinking that internal, product-analytics telemetry is somehow exempt from the same discipline because it is "just for the product team."

Events drift as the app changes, and a spec must anticipate this. Six months after launch, Charuta's design team reworked the onboarding wizard, and careplan_created started firing at a different point in the new flow — a fact nobody noticed until the activation trend line showed an unexplained jump. A mature telemetry requirement includes an app_version or event_version property precisely so a later analyst can tell whether a metric moved because user behaviour changed or because the definition underneath it silently changed.

Every event needs a human owner, not just a database column. Events fail silently — an SDK update breaks a call, a server-side filter accidentally drops a payload — and unlike a broken button, nobody notices immediately because nothing visibly stops working for the user. The owner column in Table 1 exists so that when reminder_sent volume unexpectedly halves overnight, there is a named person whose job includes noticing, not a hope that someone eventually will.

How this looks different by product type and by company stage

In a consumer product like Charuta Health, telemetry requirements cluster around a single-user funnel — install, activate, retain — because the unit of value is one person's repeated behaviour, and events are cheap and numerous: millions of app opens a day make even rare events statistically usable within days. A B2B product changes the unit of analysis: at Chaitali Systems, a fictional field-service scheduling platform sold to facilities-management firms, the meaningful telemetry is keyed to an account and a seat, not an anonymous install — an event like route_optimizer_used matters less as a raw count than as a signal of which named accounts are or are not adopting a feature ahead of renewal, so telemetry specs there are typically reviewed jointly by product and customer-success, and low event volume for a single large account can be as urgent a signal as a funnel drop-off is for a consumer app. A marketplace complicates the picture further: at Chinmayi Marketplace, a platform connecting home-service providers with households, telemetry has to be two-sided by construction — a booking_requested event on the demand side means little without a matching job_accepted event on the supply side, joined by a shared transaction identifier, because the thing the business actually needs to know is not "did a user do something" but "did the marketplace successfully match two parties," a liquidity question that a single-sided funnel cannot answer at all.

Company stage changes the machinery around the same principle. At an early-stage company, telemetry requirements are often a lightweight table in the PRD itself, events are added directly by the PM in a tool like Mixpanel or Amplitude, and the entire event catalogue might fit in one analyst's head — the discipline is mostly about writing the table down at all. At a larger company, the same requirement runs through a formal review: a data-platform team validates event schemas before they ship, a taxonomy owner rejects new event names that duplicate an existing one, and event definitions are tested in continuous integration so a code change that silently breaks medication_logged fails a build rather than a dashboard. The underlying question — what events prove this worked — never changes; only the amount of process wrapped around answering it does.

Common mistakes

"We'll add analytics after launch." The symptom is a blank or generic dashboard in the weeks after a feature ships, followed by a scramble to reconstruct behaviour from support tickets or app-store reviews — precisely what happened with the Teleconsult Booking Redesign. The underlying misunderstanding is treating telemetry as an engineering nicety rather than a requirement with the same status as any functional one. The cheapest diagnostic is procedural: check whether the PRD's success-metrics section names specific events before development starts; a metrics section with no named events attached is a promise with no mechanism behind it.

Vanity events with no usable properties. The symptom is a dashboard full of rising lines — "engagement is up" — that nobody can act on, because the events behind them (a blanket screen_viewed fired on every screen, as Charuta's original booking flow did) carry no properties that let anyone segment by step, cohort, or outcome. The underlying misunderstanding is that logging more, generically, is safer than logging less, specifically. The diagnostic is to ask of every proposed event, "what decision would change if this number moved?" — an event that survives no answer should be cut from the spec.

Defining the metric before the events that compose it. The symptom is two teams reporting two different numbers for what is supposedly the same metric — a 28.8 percent activation rate from one dashboard and a 22.4 percent rate from another, as in the worked example, with nobody able to say which is "the" number until someone traces both back to source events. The underlying misunderstanding is writing a target ("40 percent activation") as if it were self-defining. The diagnostic is to require that every metric in a PRD carry a one-line formula naming its constituent events, not just a target value.

No owner for event health. The symptom is a chart that quietly drops to near-zero and gets dismissed as "seasonality" or "a slow week" for several weeks running, when in fact an app update broke the SDK call. The underlying misunderstanding is assuming that once an event is instrumented, it stays instrumented forever without maintenance. The cheapest diagnostic is an automated alert on any named event whose daily volume falls more than roughly 30 percent against its trailing average, routed to the named owner in the telemetry table, not to a general engineering channel where it can be missed.

What good looks like

By the time Care Plan Adherence launched on 24 April 2026, the telemetry section of Ritika's PRD had been reviewed not only by Anand but by a data engineer, who flagged that condition_type needed to be treated as sensitive health data and routed to a restricted table rather than the general event warehouse, and by Faisal, who built the dashboard against dummy events two weeks before code freeze so the team could confirm every chart rendered correctly before a single real user touched the feature. On launch morning, the dashboard was live at 9 a.m., showing zero events, exactly as expected, and by 11 a.m. it was showing the first real careplan_created events arriving. On day three, the ratio of reminder_sent to medication_logged events on Android looked wrong — reminders were firing but very few were converting to logged doses on that platform specifically — and by day four, engineering traced it to a notification-tap deep link that opened the wrong screen on one Android build. The fix shipped within twenty-four hours of detection, not eleven days, because the events that would reveal the problem had been specified before the code that caused it was even written.

Closing

At her fortnightly review with Anand in early May, Ritika reported both activation numbers — 28.8 percent under the plan-creation definition, 22.4 percent under the dose-logging definition — and recommended the team adopt the stricter one as the number that went to the board, along with a roadmap item to close the 24-to-72-hour gap where the six percentage points of difference were being lost. Anand agreed, and made the telemetry table a standing item on every PRD review going forward, not because it was a trend at other companies but because Charuta Health had now felt, twice, what it costs not to have one. What Ritika resolved to study next was the event taxonomy itself — the shared vocabulary her team's events were meant to draw from — because a telemetry table written well against a weak or inconsistent taxonomy still produces events nobody else in the company can find or trust. Two questions are worth sitting with, whether or not you work anywhere near Charuta Health's kind of product: for a feature your team shipped in the last quarter, can you name the exact event and property that would prove it worked — not approximately, but exactly, the way Table 1 does? And if the definition behind your headline metric changed tomorrow, the way Ritika's activation number changed from 28.8 to 22.4 percent, would your team's priorities change with it — and if so, what does that tell you about how much weight that number was really able to bear?
