Hallikar and the Reorder Card

A decision about what a product requirements document should promise to measure

1. Opening

At 7:30 on the evening of Tuesday 20 October 2026, Prameela Avasarala, head of product at Hallikar Commerce, sat in the Bengaluru office with a draft requirements document on one screen and a video call on the other. In Pune, Praveen Achanta had stayed late. Poongodi Arumugam joined from Berlin, where it was four in the afternoon, and Phaneendra Alagiri from Toronto, where it was ten in the morning.

The draft described One-Tap Reorder, a card on a retailer's home screen that rebuilds the last order in a single tap. The sprint would be locked on Friday 23 October; anything the spec had not named by then would wait for the next one, and Diwali, on Sunday 8 November, would not. The telemetry section of the draft had one line: "Standard analytics events." Prameela had three days to decide what it should say, and how much release time it was worth (Figure 1).

2. Company background

Hallikar Commerce, founded in Coimbatore in 2021, sells groceries and household goods wholesale to kirana stores through a mobile app. Retailers in Chennai, Coimbatore, Hyderabad, Vijayawada and Bengaluru order from 14 Hallikar warehouses, pay by UPI or on short credit, and receive delivery the next morning. In the four weeks to Saturday 17 October, 18,400 retailers placed at least one order. Together they placed 57,040 orders at an average of ₹6,800, which is ₹38.79 crore of goods, of which Hallikar keeps about 2.6 per cent as net revenue.

The company has raised ₹62 crore in two rounds and employs 310 people. Its rivals are larger. Udaan, Jumbotail and Flipkart Wholesale chase the same shelves, while Reliance's JioMart Partner programme and ONDC-connected sellers court the same shopkeepers with their own apps. Hallikar's case is regional depth: Tamil and Telugu catalogues, staples from Aachi and Sakthi Masala to Amul dairy lines, and a field team that knows the stores. With margins this thin, a retailer who orders 3.1 times in four weeks instead of 2.8 matters more than a new install.

3. The situation

The thinking behind One-Tap Reorder is simple. A kirana owner buys much the same two dozen items every week, and rebuilding that basket costs five or six minutes of scrolling. Prameela's goal is to lift orders per active retailer in four weeks from 3.1 to 3.4.

She has seen what happens without a measurement plan. Hallikar Credit Line launched on Monday 13 July 2026 with no events of its own. The orders table, the system of record, shows 2.8 orders per active retailer in the four weeks before launch and 3.1 in the four weeks to 17 October. Sales credits the credit line. Praveen points to stocking for Navratri, which began on 11 October. Nobody can say whether retailers shown the credit line ordered more than those who were not, because no event recorded who saw it.

Exhibit 1 shows what the app emits today. The raw event log is kept for 45 days, so no count can reach back further, and every count here covers the four weeks from Sunday 20 September to 17 October. Nothing in the list could record whether a retailer saw a reorder card. In the log a reorder would surface inside order_placed, through its entry_point property, which was added on 14 September and has not yet carried a "reorder" value.

Figure 2 draws the path a reorder takes and the question each step asks. Phaneendra's view from Toronto is that every step deserves an event. Praveen's, from Pune, is that every event is a promise to keep firing correctly through each later release. Poongodi, in Berlin, wants to know whether anyone notices the card at all.

4. The people

Praveen Achanta, engineering lead in Pune, runs three engineers on the feature, 18 engineer-days in all. He wants a date he can keep and events specified closely enough, with trigger and properties, that his team does not argue about them in code review.

Poongodi Arumugam, senior designer in Berlin, wants the card's viewed event to fire only when half of it has been on screen for one second. She is wary of new consent screens, and Hallikar's counsel has asked that no event carry a retailer's name or phone number, in line with the Digital Personal Data Protection Act, 2023.

Phaneendra Alagiri, data scientist in Toronto, wrote the Credit Line analysis and does not want to write another like it. He wants a random holdout of 10 per cent of retailers, which is 1,840 of 18,400, and as many events as the path has steps. His mornings are Bengaluru's evenings, so a question sent at close of business is answered by the time the office reopens.

Prameela Avasarala answers to the chief executive for the festive quarter. She does not want to be asked in January whether the feature worked and have only an opinion to offer.

5. Exhibits

6. The options

Option 1: ship on the existing events. The spec keeps its one telemetry line and the 18 engineer-days go to the feature alone. The release is Tuesday 3 November, the earliest of the three, and the added cost is nil. Success is judged from the orders table, as with Credit Line. It adds no events and no comparison group.

Option 2: instrument the whole path. The spec names 14 new events, a superset of the four listed under Option 3, covering every tap, edit, dismissal and substitution, adds a streaming pipeline, and reserves a random 10 per cent holdout. The 15 extra engineer-days cost ₹2.25 lakh and, with the Diwali closure, move the release to Monday 16 November. Against a 4 November release, the 12 days of delay forgo about 2,100 orders, roughly ₹1.4 crore of goods, at the hoped-for lift across the 16,560 retailers outside the holdout.

Option 3: name only the events the success question needs. The spec adds four events (reorder_card_viewed, reorder_tapped, reorder_basket_edited and experiment_assigned), gives the "reorder" value to entry_point, and holds back a random 10 per cent. It costs 3 engineer-days, ₹0.45 lakh, and a one-day later release. The holdout withholds the card from 1,840 retailers for four weeks; at the hoped-for 0.3 extra orders each, that is 552 orders, ₹37.5 lakh of goods and ₹0.98 lakh of net revenue. It leaves other behaviour on the card unrecorded.

7. Questions for discussion

  1. Credit Line launched with no events of its own. What would Prameela have needed recorded in July to settle the argument between Sales and Praveen, and how much of it does Exhibit 1 already hold?
  2. For each step in Figure 2, what could the team decide differently on the strength of its number, and who would decide it?
  3. Compare the options in Exhibit 2 by what the team will know on 2 December and by what each costs in rupees and in days. Which differences matter most to the chief executive?
  4. What should the telemetry section say on Friday 23 October for the option you choose, and how will the team confirm on the first Friday after release that the events are firing correctly?

8. A note for the learner

Telemetry is a requirement like any other. A requirement says what the feature must do; a telemetry requirement says what it must report so that someone can tell whether it did any good. Each event in a spec needs a name drawn from the taxonomy, a trigger, its properties, an owner, the decision it feeds and a test that shows it firing. An event with no decision attached is a candidate for deletion.

A well-reasoned answer starts from the question, not the event list: do retailers who are shown the card order more than comparable retailers who are not? It then works backwards to the least that can answer it, and counts what that costs in days and rupees against the cost of not knowing.

One defensible path is Option 3. Four events and a value on an existing property cover noticing, wanting, editing and ordering, with the holdout as the comparison. The holdout is large enough: 1,840 against 16,560, with orders per retailer varying by a standard deviation of 2.4 over four weeks (taken from the orders table), gives a standard error of 0.059 orders. The smallest lift detectable at 80 per cent power and 5 per cent significance is 2.8 times that, 0.17, against the 0.3 hoped for. Diwali falls in both groups alike, whereas in a before-and-after comparison it would sit in one period.

The spec should also fix, before launch, the threshold that counts as success, the day-three check on the viewed-to-tapped ratio, and the date for revisiting the ten further events Option 2 would add if the data raises a question that needs them. That is one path; a team with a larger engineering squad, or a later Diwali, could defensibly choose differently.
